items.title: "C-295 facility represents work culture of New India," says PM Modi as he and Spanish PM inaugurate facility
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel Vadodara (Gujarat) [ India ], October 28 (ANI): Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Monday inaugurated the TATA- Airbus aircraft assembly facility complex in Vadodara. The facility will manufacture C-295 aircraft at the TATA Advanced Systems Limited campus. PM Modi said that the C-295 facility represents the work culture of a new India . "Recently, we lost the country's great son Ratan Tata ji. If he had been among us today, he would have been happy, but wherever his soul is, he would be happy. This C-295 aircraft factory reflects the new work culture of New India ... When I was the Gujarat CM, it was decided to set up a factory in Vadodara to build train coaches. The factory was also prepared for production within a record time. Today, we are exporting the metro coaches manufactured in that factory to other countries. I am confident that in the future, the aircraft made in this factory will also be exported to other countries," PM Modi said. "Today the defence manufacturing ecosystem in India is touching new heights. If we had not taken concrete steps 10 years ago, it would have been impossible to reach this level today. At that time, no one could even imagine that there could be such large-scale defence manufacturing in India . But we decided to walk on the new path, set a new goal for ourselves. And today the result is before us," PM Modi added. The Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez underlined the importance of the new industrial site. Sanchez said, "Today we are not only officially inaugurating a cutting-edge industrial facility. Today we're also witnessing how an extraordinary project between two emblematic companies becomes a reality. Prime Minister Modi, this is another triumph of your vision. Your vision is to turn India into an industrial powerhouse and a magnet for investment and business. This partnership between Airbus and Tata will contribute to the progress of the India n aerospace industry and will open new doors for the arrival of other European companies." " Tata is probably the best exponent of India n industrial strength. Its products and services are present in virtually every country on the planet. Tata is a giant among giants. As for Airbus , it embodies the very essence of a united Europe. Committed to technological innovation and the creation of jobs and prosperity. For my country, for Spain , being an integral part of the Airbus consortium, defending the values it represents. Values on which the very idea of Europe is based on cooperation, modernity and progress," Sanchez added. During the inauguration of the TATA Aircraft Complex for manufacturing C-295 aircraft, Tata Sons Chairman N Chandrasekaran announced the facility's goals. "The final aircraft assembly complex for the first aircraft to be delivered is being set up here. I must commit to our Prime Minister that exactly two years from now we will deliver the first indigenously manufactured aircraft and we will request and we'll work with your office to block the date so that you can come and inaugurate the facility and receive the first product. The first 200 engineers from Tata Group are already in Spain going through the training that is required, and we have worked with 40 SME companies and we will be adding more companies to build the entire localisation that is required for the product," he said. This collaboration between Tata Advanced Systems Ltd. (TASL) and Airbus Spain will mark India 's first private sector final assembly line (FAL) for military aircraft, boosting the nation's aerospace capabilities. The plant, located at TASL's Vadodara campus, is part of India 's Rs 2.5 billion deal signed in 2021 to acquire 56 C-295 military transport aircraft from Airbus . Under the agreement, Airbus will deliver 16 aircraft directly from Spain , while the remaining 40 will be manufactured in India by TASL. This project will create a comprehensive ecosystem for aircraft development, covering assembly, testing, certification, and maintenance throughout the lifecycle of the aircraft. Major India n defence players like Bharat Electronics Ltd (BEL) and Bharat Dynamics Ltd (BDL), along with smaller enterprises, are also contributing to this project. The C-295 aircraft will strengthen India 's Air Force fleet with a modern and more reliable transport solution. Earlier in the day, PM Modi and Sanchez participated in a roadshow in Vadodara as they headed to inaugurate Tata Advanced Systems Ltd's facility. (ANI)

items.title: "Trust but verify...," says former envoy KP Fabian on patrolling agreement between India-China along LAC
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [ India ], October 22 (ANI): KP Fabian , former India n Ambassador to Canada, struck a cautious note regarding the recent agreement between India and China on border patrolling along the Line of Actual Control ( LAC ), advising that while trust is essential, verification is equally important. While speaking with ANI, he said, "It's a very important statement that says that India and China have come to an agreement about normal patrolling and that there will be disengagement. The Foreign Secretary says that we are now looking at the resolution of the problem which arose in 2020." He added, "Some years ago, before a meeting, PM Narendra Modi was going to China for another international meeting. It (the issues) were resolved. But, let us recall that the Chinese did not carry out (the solution). The agreement was in two stages. In the first stage, India will withdraw first, then China will withdraw. That was done. In the second stage, China had to withdraw first, and then India , which they didn't do. Then, they constructed a lot of things. So, this step is welcome. Let me put it this way, trust but verify." The former diplomat further said that being neighbours, it is necessary for India and China to have "good neighbourly relations" if possible.

He said, " China is coming under a lot of pressure from the West. Americans are saying that China has been supporting Russia (with regard to the Russia-Ukraine conflict). Chinese electric vehicles are coming under high tariffs and so China is coming under pressure... And I believe that China and India , both being big countries but neighbours, it is necessary to have, if possible, good neighbourly relations." On Monday, Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri, said India and China have reached an agreement on the patrolling arrangements along LAC . The agreement was reached ahead of the BRICS Summit which will be attended by PM Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping . This is leading to disengagement and eventually a resolution of the issues that had arisen in these areas in 2020," he added. (ANI)

items.title: "No shortage of oil in world and prices should hopefully come down", says Hardeep Singh Puri
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): Hardeep Singh Puri, Minister for Petroleum and Natural Gas on Tuesday said that there is no shortage of oil in the world and prices will come down soon, answering the question of the recent upswing in crude oil prices. Speaking to the media, the Union Minister cited global factors such as the war in the Middle East and voluntary cuts in oil production which are influencing the oil prices in the global market. He said, "It depends on global factors. One thing is very clear, there is no shortage of oil in the world...Today, more and more oil is coming on the market...There are other factors like geopolitical tensions. So, there is no shortage of oil but if there is tension in one part of the world, then the freight cost, and insurance freight cost will go up. Today, let us all hope that better sense prevails, that call for peace that our Prime Minister has been making from every forum...There is more than enough oil in the world and prices should hopefully come down. That's my expectation..." "If there's tension in one part of the world, then the cost of, if you have to take a longer route, then the cost of the freight cost, the insurance rate cost, that will go up...There's more than enough oil in the world, and prices should hopefully come down," he commented in his personal capacity.

The union minister said many countries such as Brazil, and Guayana among others are coming with their oil. Citing the stable prices in the last 3 years, the minister said that the government is taking every possible step to ensure stable oil prices. "Central government at every stage has stepped in to cushion and bring the prices down from November 2021 to May 2022. Now there are some global factors. The cost at the retail point is determined by the cost of the barrel in the international market plus the cost of transportation, freight, insurance, retailers, refining cost and margin, then dealers, margin, etc. We are solving all the problems we can, now you tell the global community to hold and bring them down," he added. This comes after oil prices rose nearly 2 per cent on Monday, reclaiming major losses from last week's sell-off. Brent crude features upped by $1.44, or 1.97 per cent in the afternoon. Earlier this month, Puri had said that the country is well-prepared to meet its growing energy demands, with a diverse range of oil sources. Speaking on the availability of oil in the global market, Puri emphasised that India has expanded its procurement base, moving from 27 suppliers to 39. (ANI)

items.title: India is the top market for investment globally: Mark Mobius
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): Mark Mobius, Founder of Mobius Capital Partners LLP , and an ace investor with expertise in emerging markets said, India's is the top stock market globally where he would like to invest. In an exclusive interview with ANI, the octagenarian said, "India would have to come first when I think about investment," Mobius stated, "Of course, India would have to be the first choice. Then, I would probably look at Taiwan. It's a Chinese society, but it's a free society and they're doing very well. Now we're beginning to see China rise again. There will be some interesting companies in China, but still, India remains our top pick." Mobius highlighted technology as his favorite sector to invest in India. "In the future, I believe there's going to be significant growth in hardware technology. As you know, India is already strong in software technology, but moving forward, hardware manufacturing will gain momentum here in India," he said. Discussing India's semiconductor infrastructure, Mobius mentioned that it is already developing. "Many of the world's large semiconductor companies already have software development operations in India, employing thousands of software engineers. The next step, of course, is hardware. Soon, we'll see large semiconductor manufacturing plants. The scale of investment we're talking about isn't in the millions, but billions of dollars, to produce the most advanced semiconductors in the world." Mobius also fondly remembered Ratan Tata, who passed away this month. "I met him many years ago and found him to be a very friendly, humble, and insightful person. I was deeply saddened to hear about his passing. I considered him one of the great Indian entrepreneurs of the century," Mobius added. Earlier on Monday, Mark Mobius, speaking at the NDTV World Summit 2024, reiterated he was bullish on India's real estate and semiconductor sectors, as he outlined the potential of these two key industries. In the semiconductor space, he said fabrication companies (fabs) will come here because India has got the population and the labour force. The octagenarian believes India will become "the leader" of the semiconductor industry. The government has so far approved five semiconductor units in India, of which construction in two sites is on, and soon the work in the other three will start. The companies have already made a cumulative investment of almost Rs 1.5 lakh crore. While talking about the parameters he looks at while investing in companies, Mobius said he looks at the growth of earnings in companies, along with the return on capital invested, and the quality of management. Asked about his investment advice to his "younger self," Mobius said, "Don't be in a rush, and study carefully". He added that one has to listen to the market. (ANI)

items.title: Mukka Proteins Limited Announces Rs 98 Crore Preferential Issue for Acquisition and Expansion
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel VMPL Mumbai (Maharashtra) [India], October 22: Mukka Proteins Limited , India's largest fish meal and insect meal producer and a leader in the animal protein industry , has announced the approval of a preferential issue worth Rs 98 crore by its Board of Directors. This strategic move will help Mukka Proteins in its ongoing domestic and international acquisition and expansion efforts, reinforcing its position in the global market. A significant portion of the funding will come from the promoter and promoter group, underlining their commitment to the company's robust growth strategy. The preferential issue will comprise up to 1.96 crore equity shares at Rs50 per share, aggregating to Rs98 crore. This price includes a premium of Rs49 per share on the face value of Rs1. items.title: India to grow at 6.8 pc in FY25 and 6.6 pc in FY26: S&P Global Market Intelligence
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): India's growth, although moderating, remains strong with a forecasted average of 6.8 per cent for the fiscal year 2024-25 and 6.6 per cent for 2025-26, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence . Despite a slowdown in economic momentum due to weaker public-sector investment, the outlook for India's economy is buoyed by several positive factors. Easing inflation, favourable monsoon conditions, and increased government social spending are expected to boost household demand. Additionally, healthy corporate balance sheets are playing a vital role in supporting the recovery of private investment. S&P Global Market Intelligence has released its October Global Economic Forecast update, emphasizing a steady global economic expansion supported by policy stimulus, while acknowledging risks from geopolitical factors. The outlook highlights moderating inflation and easing monetary policies as key factors steering the global economy towards a "soft landing."

Ken Wattret, global economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence , remarked, "The global economy is on track for a soft landing, with inflation rates moderating and monetary policy easing becoming more widespread. Still, geopolitical developments have the capacity to dampen or even derail the expansion." Report forecasts an annual real GDP growth rate of 4.3 per cent in 2024 and 4.4 per cent in 2025 for the region excluding China and Japan. Aiding this growth is resilient domestic demand, as regional central banks adopt more accommodative monetary stances. The start of the US Federal Reserve's easing cycle in September is creating more room for interest rate cuts, prompting several central banks, including those in the Philippines, New Zealand, Hong Kong SAR, and Indonesia, to lower rates. S&P Global Market Intelligence underscores that while the global economic outlook remains positive, risks persist. Geopolitical tensions could potentially derail economic progress, especially in regions with heightened uncertainties. Nonetheless, policy measures aimed at stimulating growth, coupled with moderating inflation, are setting the stage for a sustained economic expansion. (ANI)

items.title: Dartmouth's provost warned us about AI cheating—but his own AI use cost him his job
paras: Disclosure Day Dartmouth’s provost warned us about AI cheating—but his own AI use cost him his job People who love AI don’t always love telling others they used it.

47 Dartmouth's New Hampshire campus. Credit: Getty Images Dartmouth's New Hampshire campus. Credit: Getty Images Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav On August 9, 2026, Dartmouth College provost Santiago Schnell wrote a Washington Post op-ed called “Universities are fighting AI cheating. But there’s a deeper problem.” This week, Schnell discovered the depths of the problem himself as he resigned from the university after an advisory committee found that he failed to disclose significant AI use in an academic paper and in the Washington Post op-ed, even though publishers required such disclosure.

Schnell didn’t make it especially easy for the committee to investigate his AI use; the report uses the term “insufficient cooperation.” He did turn over his Dartmouth laptop, but he did not turn over logs from his personal LLM accounts related to the writings in question. Nor did he agree to meet with the committee.

The committee did get access to the Claude enterprise account Schnell had used through Dartmouth, though. This shows him using the LLM as a tool for revising his papers, finding and fixing bugs in code, and editing or generating figures. For instance, Schnell would run his papers through Claude and ask things like:

I am getting read[y] to submit the enclosed paper, its supplementary materials and the enclosed repo to ChemSystemsChem. This paper is not biological, but rather chemical. Imagine that you are a reviewer for this paper with expertise in nonlinear chemical dynamics and mathematical chemical kinetics. What would be your referee report for this paper?

This is quite a bit different from asking Claude to write your entire paper for you, and Schnell has long insisted that he used AI as an editorial aid and discussion partner. He told Semafor that he had used chatbots “to refine a few arguments” and “check for grammatical errors.” He told one journal editor that he “used AI as an editorial tool” to “help refine sentences, improve clarity, and the expression of arguments.” He had not disclosed his AI use to an academic journal, he said, because he “did not understand that this type of AI-assisted editing required disclosure.”

Indeed, Schnell’s own description of what he did with AI doesn’t sound, on the long list of AI-powered sins, like it would rank near the top. But it’s hard to know. As the Dartmouth committee points out, the full scope of Schnell’s AI use was unclear to them. The committee believes that Schnell’s public statements may understate “the nature of the Provost’s actual AI use” and says that Schnell regularly “went beyond his other public descriptions of his use of AI in writing.”

We do know that Schnell also asked LLMs to take TeX files and “make the corrections to the files, and the repo. If you have to generate new figures, please provide them to me. Let me know what you change in the repo, and text files so that I can take a look into it.”

Whatever you think of his actions, Schnell repeatedly failed to disclose them. It is certainly possible that he thought his AI use was on par with a spelling or grammar checker, though one Claude exchange raises questions about whether Schnell wanted to hide traces of LLM activity in his work. From the committee report:

Provost Schnell’s Claude logs reflect that he uploaded to Claude a manuscript of a forthcoming article entitled Academic Freedom and Catholic Mission: The Procedural Overlap Zone in University Governance and prompted Claude: “Are there many signatures of AI writing in this article?” Schnell later submitted a revised manuscript that incorporated the kinds of changes Claude suggested.

Schnell has now resigned. Dartmouth, though, is barreling ahead with AI. The university calls itself the place that “launched the field of artificial intelligence” back in 1956, when “the term was coined and the foundational question was asked: Can machines solve problems once reserved for human minds?” Seventy years later, Dartmouth is hosting a conference called “What Must Remain Human?” that will feature a student hackathon sponsored by Anthropic and speakers like Mira Murati and Yann LeCun.

Despite the scandal, Dartmouth President Sian Leah Beilock wants more AI. (She wrote a piece for The Atlantic in September called “Why I Want More AI at Dartmouth.”) What’s crucial, though, is that the school’s leaders should “hold themselves to the highest standards,” she said. This appears to mean one main thing: disclosure.

In announcing Schnell’s resignation , Beilock wrote that “each of us brings a different perspective on how and when to incorporate AI into our work and our lives. Moreover, keeping Dartmouth at the forefront of AI inevitably means leading through an environment that is fluid and fast-changing. That is why, as leaders, it is so critical that we model the transparency and human judgment that we expect from our students and scholars.”

What does “disclosure” mean? In a September 2026 paper on AI detection tools, called “Who Wrote This?”, Schnell himself goes to great lengths to argue that “human-written” or “AI-written” is far too simple a binary. In his view, everything will become a mix of human judgment and AI work, and there’s nothing wrong with that. The key for him is that the human author takes full responsibility for the text, however it was composed and edited.
In the paper, Schnell lays out his method for producing it. It’s worth quoting at some length:

In September 2026, I asked OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Pro whether an AI-written essay could ever be identified with certainty, and I suggested connecting the problem to Turing’s imitation game and to the “reverse” Turing test posed by AI-text detection. GPT-5.6 Pro connected the question to binary hypothesis testing and statistical decision theory, proposed early structures and titles, identified candidate literature, and generated portions of early drafts. I chose the problem, journal, audience, and eventual direction of the argument. I decided which examples and results should remain central, including the decision to retain the Liang study while confronting it with important counterevidence. I checked the cited literature, rejected or corrected claims that I judged inaccurate, corrected mathematical and conceptual errors, and reorganized the argument.

In revising the manuscript, I rewrote most sections and added substantial explanations. I occasionally asked GPT-5.6 Sol to provide language-editing assistance for sections I had rewritten. I created the figures and made the final decisions about the mathematics, interpretation, sources, organization, and wording. I take full responsibility for the resulting manuscript.

Before submitting the manuscript for publication, I also asked GPT-5.6 Pro and Anthropic Claude Fable 5.1 to review it critically and identify issues that reviewers might raise. I evaluated the issues they identified and made corrections where I judged them warranted.

Despite all this assistance, Schnell resists the idea that AI is a “co-author.” Instead, he writes, “Calling [the paper] ‘coauthored’ would introduce a different confusion. Mathematical tools have long made substantive contributions without thereby becoming authors… The point is not that the software contributed nothing. It is that contribution and authorship are different roles.”
He is not against disclosure, as he makes clear by describing his method. Yet curiously, when submitting other papers for publication, he did not disclose his AI use even when required by publishers.

Confused about the rules in an age where even universities are pushing AI? So are many students. New survey data unveiled at this weekend’s conference shows that 61 percent of college students think AI helps explain difficult concepts, and half believe that they produce better work after talking through issues with AI tools. But “70 percent of the college students in the survey indicate that take-home work has become unfair due to AI, with 39 percent feeling pressured to use it because their peers do.” Among Dartmouth students, 92 percent of them fear “that AI can hurt writing skills.” And many of them believe their peers are using far more AI than they actually are.

Not everyone is racked with existential doubt over how to deal with AI, though. Dartmouth student Eli Moyse wrote in a September op-ed that Schnell should be fired because “a fetishization of AI to earn publicity for the College has rotted the brain of our top academic.”

items.title: Flesh-eating screwworms spread to third state and are attacking pets
paras: Real nightmare fuel Flesh-eating screwworms spread to third state and are attacking pets USDA has identified 74 animal cases in US since parasitic flies invaded in June.

33 The tip of a screwworm fly larvae. Credit: CSIRO The tip of a screwworm fly larvae. Credit: CSIRO Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav For a genuine fright this Halloween, you can turn your gaze to the southern border, where ravenous, flesh-eating maggots are festering and have taken to eating people’s pets.

This week, the country’s New World Screwworm (NWS) infestation spread to a third state, Arizona, which joins New Mexico and Texas in being plagued by the horrifying parasites. To date, 74 animal cases have been identified in the US since the flies re-invaded the country in June.

The flies lay hundreds of eggs in wounds and moist orifices of animals, and the resulting voracious maggots feast on their victims. The maggots resemble screws and tortuously bore and twist into living flesh, causing severe, sometimes fatal wounds, before dropping to the ground to develop into adults.

Because of their ability to ravage livestock, the flies were eliminated from the country in the 1960s through aerial releases of sterile male flies, which thwart successful breeding. For years, they were held at bay using a biological barrier along the Darién Gap at the border of Panama and Colombia. But the barrier was breached in 2022, and the flies have made their way back to the US through Central America.

While they are largely seen as a threat to the livestock industry, they can also devastate wildlife, domestic pets, and in rarer cases, humans . According to the latest data from Mexico’s Ministry of Health , the country has confirmed 806 cases of human screwworm infestations since the flies reemerged. Nine people died from the savage maggots.

In the US, most of the 74 confirmed cases have been in livestock. But some of the cases have been in domestic pets, mainly dogs. Just this week, the US Department of Agriculture recorded four new cases in domestic dogs—which includes the new detection in Arizona—as well as a domestic cat in New Mexico. That brings the pet total to 10 cases since the flies reemerged. The US has also detected one case in a wild elk, which was reported last week.

Arizona’s agriculture department said this week that the state’s index case was identified in a dog in Cochise County, which borders both New Mexico and Mexico. A local veterinarian examined the poor pup on October 26 and found a wound on the canine’s back that was “heavily infested with maggots consistent with NWS characteristics.”

“We remain prepared and vigilant, and we urge all livestock owners, pet owners, and other animal industry partners to continue to monitor animals closely and report any unusual wounds consistent with NWS immediately,” the state said in an announcement .
The USDA confirmed the infection and said it was working closely with Arizona on a joint response to the expanded infestation.

items.title: Oh captain, our captain: Ars staff remembers Patrick Stewart
paras: he lived long and prospered Oh captain, our captain: Ars staff remembers Patrick Stewart “For huge numbers of people, I will always be Jean-Luc Picard. … We created an admirable individual.”

48 Credit: CBS/Paramount+ Credit: CBS/Paramount+ Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav Along with the rest of the world, we at Ars are mourning Sir Patrick Stewart —the beloved award-winning actor best known as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men franchise—who died yesterday at the age of 86.

We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia. He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all. We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.

Through the actor’s X account , the family has requested that, in lieu of flowers, memorial contributions be made to the Johns Hopkins Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center Fund and the Alzheimer’s Foundation of America Caregiver Resources .

Born in Yorkshire, England, in 1940, the acting bug bit Stewart at the age of 12, when his English teacher handed out scripts for Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice and asked young Patrick to read the part of Shylock—a role the adult Stewart would later play for the Royal Shakespeare Theater (RSC), among many other parts. His signature bald head emerged early, around 19, thanks to alopecia. He briefly worked as a cub reporter and a furniture salesman before winning a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theater School, and he landed his first professional role in 1959, playing a marooned pirate in a production of Treasure Island for the Lincoln Repertory Company.

Stewart worked regularly in theater and on British television, and his big break came in his late 40s. The actor was conducting master classes on Shakespeare at the University of California, Los Angeles, when a TV producer developing TNG heard him lecture and thought he would make a perfect captain for the Enterprise-D . Creator Gene Roddenberry wasn’t initially keen on the choice, but Stewart’s audition changed his mind. The rest is television history.

On Instagram , fellow thespian Sir Ian McKellen—who first met Stewart when both were young actors with the RSC and co-starred as Magneto in the X-Men films—recalled the day Stewart told him about the Star Trek offer.

“’But Patrick, think of your stage career in the UK,'” McKellen recalled saying. “‘Do you really want to risk—getting lost in Hollywood for years and years?’ Well, he took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did.”

Stewart himself never expressed anything but pride in the role. “For huge numbers of people, I will always be Jean-Luc Picard, and that’s fine,” he told The Independent in 2003. “I really believe we created an admirable individual.”

TNG ended in 1994, but it wasn’t long before Stewart created another iconic role, starring as Professor Charles Xavier in 2000’s X-Men , alongside McKellen as Magneto. He reprised the role in six more films and voiced the character in multiple video games.

He was a serious actor who never took himself too seriously, relishing Shakespeare, Ibsen, and Beckett but also throwing himself into comedic TV appearances on Saturday Night Live, The Daily Show (he was a “special correspondent” for several segments in 2012), and Sesame Street . Who could forget his timeless “Soliloquy on B,” channeling Hamlet? Or his daily readings of Shakespearean sonnets that helped us all get through the COVID-19 pandemic? He voiced Napoleon in 1999’s Animal Farm , CIA Deputy Director Avery Bullock on American Dad and, earlier this year, Sir Nitchfield in the delightful Sheep Detectives .

In between acting gigs, Stewart found time for charity work, advocating for such causes as domestic violence prevention and PTSD awareness among members of the armed forces, drawing on his own childhood being raised by an abusive father. All of this made Stewart one of the most beloved actors of our time. Tributes to Stewart are all over social media today, as celebrities and regular folk alike reflect on everything the actor’s work has meant to them over the years, including these heartfelt words from his lifelong friend McKellen:

Before everything else, Patrick was defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire, the proud county in the north of England which he loved to the end. You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues. He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love.
Ars staffers share their own reminiscences about Stewart and what he meant to them below.

I had the good fortune to literally bump into Sir Patrick Stewart outside Bond 45 in Midtown Manhattan (when it was on 45th Street). I was coming out of the restaurant with a couple of colleagues one evening when I turned right into him. When my eyes met his, I entered a state of total confusion. I knew he loved and even played Broadway, but it didn’t register why he was here, right next to me.

Fortunately, I recovered—but then, for some unknown reason, I said in a pirate voice, “Scuse muh, Capt’n!” But he didn’t miss a beat, smiled, and took a posture of “after you good sir!” I immediately chuckled like a fool and then added that I loved his work both on and off the stage. He thanked me, and we kept on rolling. I am thankful to this day that I didn’t say something corny like “two to beam up.”

What struck me about the exchange was that, as brief as it was, he did not appear annoyed in the slightest. And while I know he is a world-class actor, he also seemed genuinely appreciative of the comment. I am grateful today that I got to share my appreciation with him, awkward though it was.

Stewart created yet another iconic sci-fi character as Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men franchise. 20th Century Fox A very old and ill Charles Xavier appeared in 2017’s Logan . 20th Century Fox A very old and ill Charles Xavier appeared in 2017’s Logan . 20th Century Fox Stewart’s final appearance as Charles Xavier will be in Avengers: Doomsday in December. Marvel Studios Stewart’s final appearance as Charles Xavier will be in Avengers: Doomsday in December. Marvel Studios Eric Berger, senior space editor:

Warmth. Humanity. Decency. Honesty. Integrity. Intellectualism. These are but a few of the traits I associate with Captain Jean-Luc Picard. At a time when our leadership in the United States, and many other countries around the world, regularly showcases the opposite of these characteristics, is it any wonder that we dearly miss the captain of the Enterprise-D ? Picard first graced our TV screens in the late 1980s, a super impressionable time for me. As a result, for a time, that is how I expected most leaders would behave. Alas, no.

I’m sure everyone has their favorite Picard scenes, but for me it came at the very end of The Next Generation ; we had all gotten to know and love the bridge crew so well, and it felt so bittersweet that it all was ending. There was Jean-Luc, who had maintained his professional distance for seven years, joining his crew at the poker table. And now, not just the series is over, but so too is the era in which Patrick Stewart was alive and making the world a better place. It’s a little darker outside.

With Patrick Stewart’s death, there will be plenty of people remembering all of the Star Trek: The Next Generation moments when he ably portrayed Captain Picard as the moral and diplomatic core of the show. And for sure, Stewart’s meaty and memorable monologues in episodes like The Drumhead , The First Duty , Darmok , Chain of Command , and more will be long remembered by sci-fi fans and studied by actors honing their craft.

But the most lasting Captain Picard moments for me are often the ones where Stewart got to let his hair down (so to speak) and show some rare emotional vulnerability in what was usually such a composed and professional character.

I’ll remember watching Picard wrestling with and crying to his brother after the trauma of being overtaken by the Borg, or chasing a dream-world grandson around on his hands and knees . I’ll remember the pain in Stewart’s eyes after a psychic implant revealed his true feelings for Dr. Crusher or when he was forced to struggle with the weight of sending a new romantic interest and subordinate on a dangerous mission . I’ll remember countless small moments like Picard downing a shot of Aldebaran whiskey with a time-shifted Scottie, being duly chagrined by a Captain Picard Day banner during a video call with an admiral, or pretending to be the barber while thwarting smugglers on an otherwise empty ship.

It’s these smaller emotional character moments—and Stewart’s ability to make so much of them—that added depth and roundness to Captain Picard’s character over the years. And that continued all the way up to Next Generation ‘s very final moments , where Stewart captures the wistfulness and regret of Picard finally deciding to join the senior staff poker game. “Five card stud, nothing wild… and the sky’s the limit.”

As a very casual Star Trek viewer, I only really began to grasp the depth of Patrick Stewart’s acting when I became enthralled by the silver screen chemistry between him and co-star Ian McKellen in the X-Men film franchise. The love-hate relationship and emotional vulnerability that Stewart and McKellen instilled in their roles as old-friends-turned-rivals has resonated with me throughout the years, and I still have deep appreciation for how the actors’ real-life friendship grew from that acting experience.

I also count myself extremely fortunate to have seen Stewart and McKellen perform together in a Broadway stage revival of the play Waiting for Godot in 2014. I’m sad they won’t be performing together again, but whenever they had the opportunity, they shone brightly indeed.
Hope and altruism are central themes in Stewart’s iconic roles, and they resonated most with me during one of my lowest moments.

Ever the one to inspire, Stewart’s role as Professor X in many X-Men films encouraged people and mutants to see the best in themselves and in each other. In 2014’s Days of Future Past , his pep talk extended to new ears: a younger, disillusioned version of himself (played by James McAvoy), and he may have well been speaking to me, too. Professor X’s telepathic abilities transcend space, time, and reality—don’t question it too much.

Upon the film’s release, I was freshly laid off from my hometown newspaper after the copy desk saw its numbers cut in half. (What was already a skeleton crew became less than that.) It wasn’t lost on me that being a cynic and malcontent was partly why I wasn’t picked to remain at the paper. In my late 20s, I questioned many of the decisions that set me on my journalism path, unsure what would happen to my career.

The younger Charles Xavier finds himself in a similar spot: angry with himself, with other people, and with the general state of things—and he’s seemingly out of a job. The older Professor X reminds his younger self that people can overcome their self-defeating flaws. “Just because someone stumbles and loses their way doesn’t mean they’re lost forever.”

Younger Chuck laments being tormented by people’s accounts of their pain, something a person who reads the news for a living can relate to. I try to unplug from Cerebro—er, my computer—when I’m off the clock. Xavier doesn’t have that luxury. The constant voices have driven him to despair and left him increasingly jaded.
But older Xavier calls him out, saying it’s his own mindset that’s holding him back. “We need you to hope again,” he says.

Therein lies the answer to Xavier’s malady: hope. And, as it turns out, the advice was also applicable to a young journalist in a crumbling industry. Incidentally, Stewart also found himself at a career crossroads as a young man, though he wasn’t too far along a chosen path, according to the Hollywood Reporter .

At 15, he got a job at the local newspaper, The Dewsbury Reporter, where he was tasked with interviewing bereaved family members when someone in town died. Journalism turned out not to be his passion, and he spent much of his free time with drama groups. His editor finally told him he had to choose between acting and journalism—and he quit on the spot.
Maybe if I had an Englishman’s commanding baritone, I would have made the same choice.

CBS Paramount Ryan Whitwam, senior technology reporter:

Patrick Stewart was a prolific actor, but I will always associate him most with Jean-Luc Picard on Star Trek: The Next Generation , a show that made a real impression on me as a nerdy kid. It was refreshing to see a leader who valued science and reason—someone who didn’t immediately reach for their phaser. Despite the sometimes silly sci-fi subject matter, Stewart never seemed like he was too good to be spouting technobabble, even though he was famously skeptical of the role at first. Stewart’s portrayal of Picard elevated the series and helped it to age into a classic that I (and I’m sure many of you) still enjoy.

I also appreciate that he took so many different roles in movies and TV during his post-Trek career. Whenever I saw Patrick Stewart pop up on my screen or heard his voice unexpectedly come out of a cartoon character, it was a reminder of how happy TNG made me over the years. I’ll miss that, and I’ll miss knowing that Patrick Stewart is out there being a kind, thoughtful guy off screen.

The version of Patrick Stewart that lives in my head will most often be the noble starship captain who taught us life lessons every Friday night at 7 pm on channel 39. But while Stewart was obviously fantastic at portraying Picard’s stentorian and often stuffy formality, I was surprised when I discovered that the man behind the uniform was… surprisingly hilarious.

I tuned into his early 1994 Saturday Night Live appearance expecting an endless series of Trek riffs, but what I got instead was a sketch about an erotic cake shop run by a weirdly scatological baker. My confusion gave way to giggles—it was a one-note joke, but the image of Stewart in an apron talking about “sexy cakes” has stuck in my head for decades. He committed to it every bit as hard as he committed to following the Prime Directive, and at 16, it made me realize that anyone who could go from “The first duty of a Starfleet officer is to the truth!” to that and sell them both with equal intensity and sincerity was not a one-note actor. This was a man with a hell of a lot of range!

The performance that brought me the most joy, though, was his turn on Ricky Gervais’ Extras , where he played a version of himself as an actor, delivering career advice to Gervais. The scene is a masterclass in expectation subversion, something Stewart often seemed to revel in. I won’t spoil it for the two or three readers who still haven’t had the pleasure, but I will say that to this day my wife and I still say, “I’ve seen everything, I’ve seen it all!” at each other regularly in conversation.

Like many Gen Xers, I grew up loving the original Star Trek series. But The Next Generation held a special place in my heart. From the moment it premiered, I was captivated by the mind-bending concepts it explored. Jean-Luc Picard quickly became one of my favorite characters. I admired his intelligence, leadership, and moral integrity. He was the quintessential Starfleet captain, and he made balding cool in a way only Michael Jordan could rival.
Years later, I discovered what would become my favorite Patrick Stewart performance: his formidable portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge on Broadway and in the 1999 adaptation of A Christmas Carol .

For me, the movie remains the definitive version of Dickens’ classic, and watching it has become a cherished family holiday tradition. During the COVID lockdowns, we eagerly tuned in to Stewart’s readings of Shakespeare, and of course, his solo multipart rendition of A Christmas Carol . A roaring fire, some warm drinks, and his perfect Shakespearean accent made everything seem right with the world.

Growing up in the US, raised by Brits, there was something quietly thrilling about seeing a Yorkshireman handed the captain’s chair. Better still, it made TNG legitimate in the eyes of my parents—a classically trained Shakespearean actor wouldn’t be involved in anything unserious, surely. As I came of age in 2000, there he was again as Professor X. Of course he was. Who else could it have possibly been? Beyond the roles, though, he just seemed to be a genuinely good man, the Mr. Rogers and Weird Al tier of human being. And when the world was upside down at the height of COVID, there he was, reading me a daily sonnet.
